Homework 2: Corner and Blob Detection

In this assignment, you will generate simple images containing black squares on a white background and apply different operators for corner and blob detection. You will compare Harris, Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG), and Difference of Gaussian (DoG) detections across smoothing scales and image resolutions. Submission: upload hw2.zip containing hw2.py, hw1.py, and hw2.pdf if you submit handwritten answers. Keep these files in the same folder before creating the ZIP. For every short-answer question, show all steps and explain your reasoning. You may write your answer in the notebook's Markdown cell using LaTeX, or, if you prefer handwriting, include your written solutions in a PDF named exactly hw2.pdf. Clearly label each problem in the PDF and write "See hw2.pdf, Problem [number]" in the corresponding Markdown answer cell. Illegible work will receive a zero. Rules: use your Homework 1 functions laplacian, convolve2d_full, and harris_corners. Do not use np.convolve, scipy, or cv2.

Problem 1: Eigenvalues of the Structure Matrix

In Homework 1, the Harris detector used ||(R = \det(A) - k\,\bigl(\operatorname{trace}(A)\bigr)^2||) without computing the eigenvalues of the structure matrix ||(A||). Here you compute them directly. ||[ A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \qquad A_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \qquad A_3 = \frac{1}{1000}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \qquad A_4 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ||]

1(a) Structure Matrix

In the structure_matrices cell below, assign the four matrices given above as nested lists.

1(b) Eigenvalues and Feature Types

Solve ||(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0||) by hand for each matrix and show your derivation in the Markdown answer cell below. Report both eigenvalues and use them to justify whether the matrix represents a corner, edge, flat region, or an invalid structure matrix. Use an eigenvalue threshold of 1 and state the assumptions behind your classification, including what makes a structure matrix valid. Do not use code or np.linalg for this part. Show all steps. Answer in the Markdown cell below using LaTeX, or handwrite your solution in hw2.pdf, clearly labeled with the problem number. If you use the PDF, write "See hw2.pdf, Problem [number]" in the Markdown answer cell.

Your answer to Problem 1(b). A structure matrix is valid if both eigenvalues are non-negative. A1:
  • eigenvalues: 6, 0
  • Edge
A2:
  • eigenvalues: 8, 7
  • Corner
A3:
  • eigenvalues: 0.001 (multiplicity 2)
  • Flat
A4:
  • eigenvalues: 4, -2
  • Invalid

1(c) Classify Feature

Complete classify_feature(structure) using your eigenvalue derivation from 1(b). Compute the eigenvalues directly (no np.linalg), then return "corner", "edge", "flat", or "invalid".

At each offset ||(x||), the value should be the Gaussian ||(G_\sigma(x)||). Normalize the vector so its entries sum to 1. 2(d) Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG)

The Laplacian of Gaussians can be used for detecting the location of "blobs" in images. In this problem, we will apply the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operator at the same ||(\sigma \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}||) values used for Harris. Complete log_response(image, sigma) to compute the Laplacian of Gaussian response. First smooth image using your gaussian_smooth(image, sigma) function, then apply the Homework 1 Laplacian kernel using convolve_same. Return a 2D response array with the same shape as the input image.

Complete local_extrema(response, fraction) to find strong local maxima and minima. Compare absolute response values, skipping the outermost row and column. Include a pixel when both conditions hold:
  • Its magnitude is at least that of all 8 neighbours. Include ties, allowing a tolerance of ||(10^{-9}\max|\text{response}|||).
  • Its magnitude is at least fraction times the largest magnitude anywhere in the response.
Return an integer array of (row, column) coordinates with shape (N, 2), including shape (0, 2) when no pixels qualify. Choose a default fraction between 0 and 1.

2(e) Difference of Gaussian (DoG)

We can approximate the LoG using a DoG. To do this, we apply the Difference of Gaussian (DoG) operator using the same ||(\sigma||) values, with ||(k \approx 1.4||) between the two smoothing scales. Complete dog_response(image, sigma, k=1.4) using your gaussian_smooth function. Problem 3: Multi-Scale Blob and Corner Detection (Image 2)

Consider the 512×512 Image 2 from 2(a), with four black squares of different fixed sizes. This problem will help you understand the relationship between image pyramids, the Gaussian scale-space, and blob or corner detection using the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) and the Difference of Gaussian (DoG). Reuse your functions from Problems 1 and 2.

3(a) Gaussian Smoothing and Pyramid Construction

First, complete downsample(image, factor) to keep every factor-th row and column, starting at row 0 and column 0. For example, factor 2 turns a 512×512 image into a 256×256 image.

Next, implement build_scale_pyramid(image, sigmas) to return (smoothed, levels), two lists in the same order as sigmas: smoothed[i] is gaussian_smooth(image, sigmas[i]), and levels[i] is smoothed[i] downsampled by int(sigmas[i]). The preview below displays the smoothed images (top) and the pyramid levels (bottom).

3(b) Harris Corners at Multiple Scales

Using the images generated in 3(a), compute the Harris corner response at each smoothing scale ||(\sigma \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}||). We'll compare two approaches:
  1. Harris detector on the full-resolution, smoothed images (pure scale-space analysis).
  2. Harris detector on the corresponding downsampled images (pyramid representation).
Complete image_2_corners(image, threshold, max_corners) by calling your Homework 1 harris_corners, handling the white image border as in 2(c). Choose default values and use them for both approaches. The preview below runs both approaches and lists the number of corners and their median Harris response ||(R||).

In the answer cell: discuss how corner locations, counts, and strengths vary between these two approaches. Show all steps. Answer in the Markdown cell below using LaTeX, or handwrite your solution in hw2.pdf, clearly labeled with the problem number. If you use the PDF, write "See hw2.pdf, Problem [number]" in the Markdown answer cell.
Your answer to 3(b). Double-click this cell to write your answer. You may replace everything here.

3(c) Laplacian-of-Gaussian (LoG) on the Gaussian Pyramid

Using the Gaussian pyramid constructed in 3(a), compute the Laplacian-of-Gaussian response for each pyramid level. Each level corresponds to a downsampled version of the image that has been smoothed with a Gaussian of increasing ||(\sigma||). For each level, evaluate the LoG at the same nominal smoothing scales ||(\sigma \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}||), relative to that level's resolution. Detect local extrema (both maxima and minima) that correspond to blob centres. Visualize the strongest responses as circles centred at the detected locations, with radii proportional to the effective ||(\sigma||) in the original image coordinates.
Note: The Laplacian-of-Gaussian (LoG) response can be computed in two conceptually different ways:
  1. On the original full-resolution image at multiple smoothing scales ||(\sigma||) (pure scale-space analysis), where only the filter scale changes, not the image sampling.
  2. On the Gaussian pyramid, where each level is both smoothed and downsampled. This approach, used in practice by methods such as SIFT, provides a computationally efficient approximation to the continuous scale-space while capturing the effects of both scale and resolution.
In this exercise, the LoG is applied to each downsampled pyramid level to explore how feature detection behaves under changes in both image scale and sampling resolution.
First, compute effective_sigma(factor, sigma). A level downsampled by ||(f||) was already smoothed at ||(\sigma = f||) in original pixels, and filtering it at ||(\sigma||) level pixels adds a blur of ||(f\sigma||) original pixels. Gaussian variances add, so the effective scale in original-image pixels is ||[ \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{f^2 + (f\sigma)^2}. ||]

Next, complete pyramid_extrema(levels, factors, sigmas, method="log"). For every level (with downsampling factor f) and every ||(\sigma||) in sigmas, compute the response with log_response(level, sigma), or with dog_response(level, sigma) when method="dog" (used in 3(d)). Find its strongest local extrema, both maxima and minima, with your local_extrema from 2(d). For every extremum, append the row (row, column, f, sigma_eff), where (row, column) is in level pixels. Return a floating-point array of shape (N, 4). The preview cell below draws each LoG extremum on Image 2 as a circle of radius ||(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}||) centred at ||((f \cdot \text{row}, f \cdot \text{column})||).

3(d) Mapping and Visualization

Map the detected feature points back to the coordinate system of the original image. The visualization code below is provided for reference and calls your to_original function to overlay the detections. Complete to_original(points, factor) to map (N, 2) (row, column) points in a level downsampled by factor to original-image pixels. For example, (10, 15) at factor 2 maps to (20, 30).
